card.say: Honestly, I didn't have production proof of the cause. The repro device showed the late result, but that only proves it can happen. In production I'd look for the wrong price on the same SKU after a quick date change, and check whether the price shown matched the older date. updates: I'd add a small counter for dropped stale results, and log the SKU and the date when it fires. If that counter is high on the devices with wrong-price reports, and the reports stop after the fix, that's real evidence. Without those numbers, I'd say the fix is likely, not proven.

I'd check the timing, not just the count: if the wrong price always shows the older date's price, that points to a late result rather than a bad index. I'd also compare the wrong-price rate before and after the fix on the same app version, and if it drops to near zero that's strong evidence. Without those numbers I'd call the fix likely, not proven.

One more signal I'd use: the wrong price should only appear right after a fast tap. If it also shows up when the user waits, the cause is probably the index, not a late result. And I'd check the same SKU on a fast phone and a slow one. If it only happens on slow devices, that fits a late result too.

I'd also check the crash-free and ANR numbers on those devices, because a slow phone is where a late result shows up. If the wrong-price reports come from the slowest devices, that fits the late-result cause. And I'd keep the request id in the log for a few weeks after the fix, so I can still trace any new report.
I'd also cap the counter's cardinality by logging only a hashed request id, so the added logging can't itself become a memory or storage problem on low-end devices.
I'd keep the old result path behind a flag for a week, and if the wrong-price reports drop only when the flag is on, that's the strongest proof I can get without a full rollout.
I'd also watch the memory and storage cost of the new logging on low-end devices, since a per-SKU counter can grow fast if the SKU set is large.
I'd also keep the counter in memory only, not on disk, and accept that it resets on restart since it's just a signal.

I'd also set a threshold on the counter before I trust it: if the dropped-stale-result count stays near zero on the slow devices that reported wrong prices, that would actually argue against the late-result cause rather than for it.
